From a White Paper to a Working Platform: Peripateticware 2007–2026

If students follow their curiosity through real places, learning about arches, barrels, and celestial navigation because they’re standing near a cathedral or a harbour, how do you assess what they’ve learned in a way that satisfies curriculum requirements? How do you produce the spreadsheet of numbers the principal wants while also honouring the complexity of what the student actually understood?

Peripateticware doesn’t fully solve the chaos — that tension is real and probably permanent. What it does is give teachers enough structure to stay sane (designed activities, learning targets, completion phases, teacher approval workflows) while giving students enough freedom to actually go somewhere (GPS-triggered content, student-proposed activities, self-directed field notes, peer projects).

That’s a harder sell. Schools are risk-averse. Outdoor learning has a liability optic. “The world is your classroom” sounds like a marketing line until you’ve watched a ten-year-old explain sediment transport to a crow-shaped AI guide while standing in a creek bed, and then read the field journal entry they wrote that afternoon, and understood that they understood.

That’s where Peri comes in. Peri is Peripateticware’s AI guide — named, like the software, after the Aristotelian method. Peri doesn’t answer questions. It asks them. It follows the five-phase inquiry sequence — Engage, Observe, Analyse, Explain, Apply — that Aristotle used in the Lyceum and that cognitive science has since validated as a path to genuine understanding, not just retention. Peri takes a student’s observation and asks the next right question. When the student gets it right, Peri tests the implication. When the student is vague, Peri asks for evidence.
The 2007 document named one obstacle it couldn’t solve:

The 2007 paper described a “choose your own adventure” model of learning — one where students follow tangents, pursue what interests them, and encounter core curriculum concepts through the side doors of genuine curiosity rather than the front door of instruction. The paper acknowledged this was “somewhat chaotic” and that it would require new kinds of instructional design, new assessment tools, and teachers willing to trade some control for authentic engagement.
The 2026 Answer: AI Did What Spreadsheets Couldn’t

The assessment problem turned out to have two parts. The first was capturing evidence — what did the student actually observe, and can you prove it? The second was evaluating it — did their thinking deepen, or did they just describe what they saw?

The document left that question open. The school system didn’t solve it either. For nearly two decades, “outdoor learning” remained either a vague aspiration or a logistical nightmare — teachers with clipboards, activities that produced no artifact, experiences that disappeared the moment students came back inside.

The first part was solved by smartphones. Photo, audio, GPS coordinates, timestamps — a student at a creek bank can capture more evidence in ten minutes than a field trip clipboard could hold in a day. What remained was the second part: structured inquiry that didn’t just document experience but deepened it.

The longer answer is that educational technology spent those years solving the wrong problem. EdTech iterated on the classroom — better LMS, better video, better quiz tools. It made the existing model more efficient. Peripateticware doesn’t try to make the classroom more efficient. It tries to replace the classroom, at least occasionally, with the world.

The paper was written at a moment when 3G hadn’t fully rolled out, the iPhone was months away from launch, and “app” wasn’t yet a common word. Its predictions — that cell phones would become 1-for-1 classroom devices, that mobile networks would reach remote regions, that GPS would become cheap enough to put in every student’s pocket — all came true. The products the paper called for did not.

The result is an artifact: a field journal entry with captures, extended analysis, and a record of the inquiry itself. Teachers can see not just what a student concluded but how they got there. Rubrics aligned to Bloom’s taxonomy and standards frameworks — CCSS, NGSS, TEKS, or your own — make the assessment legible to any curriculum coordinator. The spreadsheet and the real learning finally occupy the same document.

The reverse scavenger hunt — where students propose an activity based on something they found — is the closest thing in the platform to that 2007 vision. A student finds a peculiar rock formation. They propose it as an activity. The teacher approves it. Other students go look. Questions emerge that no curriculum document anticipated. Learning moves.

The short answer is that most of the enabling technology wasn’t ready in 2007. GPS in every pocket came first (2010–2015). Then high-quality mobile cameras. Then cloud APIs cheap enough for schools. Then local AI models (Ollama, llama.cpp) that can run on a teacher’s home server without a $10,000/month inference bill. The 2007 paper was right about the destination; it couldn’t have known how long the road would be.
The white paper is still online.

Privacy rules are versioned and deployed server-side. When a jurisdiction updates its requirements, the platform applies the new rule without any code change on your end.
California Consumer Privacy Act. Applies to California residents. Students and parents can request disclosure, deletion, or opt-out of sale of personal information at any time.
Granular consent capture for students, parents, and school administrators. Consent records are timestamped and auditable.
Children’s Online Privacy Protection Act. Applies to users under 13 in the United States. Parental consent is obtained before any personal data is collected from minors.

Peripateticware’s Privacy Engine is active from day one. No configuration required for standard frameworks — FERPA, COPPA, GDPR, and CCPA are enabled automatically based on the student’s detected jurisdiction.
Privacy compliance built in, not bolted on.

Need a jurisdiction-specific rule? Administrators can author and publish custom privacy rules scoped to any region, school, or organisation.
All student captures — photos, audio, GPS coordinates — are encrypted at rest and in transit using AES-256. Keys are scoped per organisation and rotated annually.

When a student submits evidence, the engine identifies their jurisdiction, loads the active compliance ruleset, applies retention and encryption policies, and stores the data accordingly — automatically.
Administrators can author custom privacy rules using a simple JSON schema. Rules can target any jurisdiction, data category, or user role.
Family Educational Rights and Privacy Act. Governs access to student education records in US schools. Student data is never shared without written consent from the school or parent.
General Data Protection Regulation. Applies to schools and students in the European Union. Data is processed only under lawful bases; students and parents hold full access and deletion rights.

The engine detects the student’s location and activates the appropriate compliance rules automatically. GDPR for EU students, FERPA and COPPA for US students, PIPEDA for Canada — with no manual configuration.
Sensitive data is processed on-device where possible. GPS coordinates are hashed before transmission. Audio and images are stored locally until the student explicitly submits them.
Peripateticware complies with COPPA, GDPR, FERPA, CCPA, PIPEDA, LGPD, and PDPA. Student data is never sold, never used for advertising, and never shared without consent.
